content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.zoroastrian-avesta-yasna-gathas-mills-archive-l5599-l5680","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/zoroastrian/project-gutenberg/zend-avesta-part-3-yasna-gathas.md","passage_locator":{"label":"YASNA    XXXII.  65 / YASNA    XXXII.  67 / F   2 / YASNA    XXXIII.  69; lines 5599-5680","start":"5599","end":"5680","translation":"The Zend-Avesta, Part III: The Yasna, Visparad, Afrinagan, Gahs, and Miscellaneous Fragments","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"Mills' commentary on Yasna XXXIII.3–6 explains that the liturgical reciter is instructed to pray for a spiritually enlightened and industrious friend who will care for cattle and work both in physical pastures and in the \"spiritual pastures\" of Divine Benevolence where a mystic kine grazes. The commentator argues that Zarathustra is the likely first-person speaker of the surrounding verses, composing a text to be recited by others, and that he is described as a \"best one\" to various social classes but not a comforter of the wicked. In line with what Mills calls practical dualism, the speaker abjures disobedience to God, arrogance, discontent, dishonesty, and neglect of sacred duties to cattle that share the sanctity of a soul, contrasting this severity with the \"lying\" of an opposed religion and linking it to the Persian reputation for truthfulness and avoidance of debt reported by Herodotus. The speaker further portrays himself as one who rejects such sins and invokes personified Obedience toward God, seeking not many years of booty and worldly glory but a long life in a kingdom founded in Divine Benevolence and in rigidly straight paths of moral purity where Ahura dwells. He longs to know from the Best Spirit (Spenta Mainyu) what should be done for the recovery and perfection of the fields, which Mills connects to an earlier plea from the soul of the kine for good pasturage that only a \"sacred agriculturist\" and diligent tiller—the typical saint—can provide. Agricultural work such as reclaiming, irrigating, and cultivating land is ranked among the highest human services, and the last preparation of gathered grain is said to make the Daevas start, shriek, and flee. Living from the fruits of the earth is contrasted with living by murderous theft, and knowledge of wise agricultural policy and means of preventing bloody freebooting is described as a supremely wise desire, worthy of a sight of Mazda and consultation with Him. This right ordering of fields and society is said to involve Ahura's personified Immortals—Righteous Order, Benevolence, Power, and Piety—whose activity in turn secures the rewarding personifications Welfare and Immortality.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"The reciter is instructed to pray for a sincere and useful friend (vahi.rta) for the believer, regardless of whether the believer is a chief, allied peer, or villager.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"The desired friend is described as spiritually enlightened, keen, persevering, and brave in the cultivation of cattle.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"This friend is said to be asked for by the Lord himself and to be needed by the Kine.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"The prayer asks that this friend be supported in his holy toil, tilling and tending not only in the pastures of the valleys but also in the spiritual pastures of the Divine Benevolence where a mystic kine is grazing.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"The commentator states that the composer resumes a first-person \"I who\" form, and argues that Zarathustra is probably the speaker of these lines, composing a piece to be recited by another.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"Zarathustra is described as a \"best one\" for people of each class but as not a comforter of the wicked.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"A prayer beginning in verse 3 is said to continue until verse 6 and to gain force with each preceding profession of fidelity.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"The commentator characterizes the passage as expressing a practical dualism, in which the speaker first abjures disobedience to God, arrogance, discontent, and dishonesty toward humans, linked with neglect of duties toward cattle that share the sanctity of a soul.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"This practical severity is contrasted with the more facile \"lying\" of an opposed religion, and is suggested as a cause of the Persian reputation for veracity, which Herodotus associates with avoiding debt.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"The speaker claims to abjure disobedience, insolence, complaint, and lying, and to invoke the great genius who is Obedience toward God.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"Through his abjuration and prayer, the speaker aims not at \"a hundred autumns\" of booty and glory but at a long life in a kingdom established in the spirit of Divine Benevolence and at rigidly straight paths of moral purity in which Ahura dwells.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"The speaker describes himself as an invoker who is \"straight\" like these paths and who seeks with longing to know from the Best Spirit, animated by the best mind, what should be done for the recovery and perfection of the fields.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:3","ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:13","text":"The commentator notes that the same term for \"pasturage\" or agriculture (vastrya) earlier described the original want of the kine's soul, which implored good pasturage (vohu vastrya) as its salvation.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:14","text":"A \"sacred agriculturist,\" described as a diligent tiller of the earth, is said to be the only one who can provide the salvation requested by the kine's soul and is presented as the typical saint.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:15","text":"The agriculturist's deeds of reclaiming, irrigating, and cultivating land are ranked among the first services of a human being.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:16","text":"The last preparation of the gathered grain is said, perhaps humorously, to make the Daevas start, shriek, and flee, as referenced from the Vendidad.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:17","text":"Living from the fruits of the earth is presented as the main difference between those who live by murderous theft and those who live honestly in the same regions.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:18","text":"Knowledge of a true policy in agriculture is described as one of the wisest possible desires and as especially worthy of a sight of Mazda and of consultation with Him.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:19","text":"The ordering of the fields and the prevention of bloody freebooting are said to involve Ahura's Righteous Order, Benevolence, Power, and Piety, called energising Immortals, and to secure the rewarding personifications Welfare and Immortality.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]}],"figures":[{"id":"fig:1","name_or_label":"Ahura (the Lord, Mazda)","description":"Supreme deity who prescribes qualities for the helpful friend, dwells in rigidly straight paths of moral purity, is consulted for wise policy, and whose Spirit and Immortals govern the kingdom and agricultural order.","role_refs":["role:1"],"evidence_refs":["ev:1","ev:3","ev:4"]},{"id":"fig:2","name_or_label":"Zarathustra (Zarathurtra)","description":"Prophet identified by the commentator as the likely first-person speaker saying \"I who,\" composing a prayer to be recited by another, abjuring sin, invoking Obedience, and seeking divine guidance for the fields.","role_refs":["role:2"],"evidence_refs":["ev:2","ev:3","ev:4"]},{"id":"fig:3","name_or_label":"Reciter of the prayer","description":"Unspecified liturgical reciter who is made to pray for a spiritually enlightened friend for the believer using the composed text.","role_refs":["role:3"],"evidence_refs":["ev:1","ev:2"]},{"id":"fig:4","name_or_label":"Believer","description":"Generic believer, of any social class, on whose behalf the reciter prays for a sincere and useful friend.","role_refs":["role:4"],"evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"fig:5","name_or_label":"Vahi.rta content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.zoroastrian-avesta-yasna-gathas-mills-archive-l3325-l3426","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/zoroastrian/project-gutenberg/zend-avesta-part-3-yasna-gathas.md","passage_locator":{"label":"YASNA    XXVIII.  19 / YASNA    XXVIII.  21 / YASNA    XXVIII. / YASNA    XXX.  25; lines 3325-3426","start":"3325","end":"3426","translation":"The Zend-Avesta, Part III: The Yasna, Visparad, Afrinagan, Gahs, and Miscellaneous Fragments","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"Mills’s commentary on Yasna XXX describes the hymn’s composer as a sage who instructs throngs seeking spiritual light. The hymn continues questions about the world’s origin and declares God’s counsels on the origin of good and evil, praises, liturgical formulae (Mathra), and sacrifices, with a prayer for propitious heavenly signs. The audience is told that a decisive moment has come for each individual to choose their religion, listening attentively and gazing at the holy Fire with a receptive mind. The commentary then expounds an early doctrine of dualism: two original spirits or forces, initially described as a better and a worse principle, later personified as independent beings. They come together to produce the opposing phenomena of life and non‑life, Heaven and Hell, where Hell is “the worst life” and Heaven “the best mental state.” The system is described as abstract, with the two beings remaining distinct even in union; having created two principles, each chooses a realm, Ahura choosing the righteous religious order and the pious of all ages, and the evil spirit choosing the wicked. Mills emphasizes that a good God cannot be responsible for permanent evil; imperfection and suffering are original and inherent, and evil is the work of an independent evil being or “evil God.” He notes that the name Angra Mainyu is absent here. The commentary then turns to historical and moral reflections: war feuds and theological animosity exceeded the sage’s philosophy, and Daeva‑worshippers are portrayed as having failed in discernment. As they deliberated, the “Worst Mind,” described as an abstract Satan, came upon them and induced them to choose his evil realm, leading them to furious intent to injure human life. Mills interprets this as a dramatic yet philosophically framed temptation and fall, and he briefly compares a later, more mythic account of Zarathustra’s own temptation with the temptation narrative in the Christian Gospels.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"The hymn’s composer is described as accustomed to instruct the masses who throng him on public occasions seeking light, and he constructs this hymn for similar opportunities.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"The composer is said to continue thoughts from Yasna XXVIII, where he had besought Ahura to inform him concerning the origin of the world.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"He declares that he will set forth the counsels of God, meaning doctrines on the origin of good and evil, together with praises, parts of the Mathra, and the sacrifices, and he prays that propitious results may be discerned in the heavenly bodies.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"The composer tells the throngs before him that a decisive moment is upon them and that they are to choose their religion individually, not by mob acclamation.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"He urges his audience to rouse themselves, listen with full attention, and gaze at the holy Fire with a good and receptive disposition of mind.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"The commentary describes an earliest statement of dualism in which there were two original spirits, characterized first as a better principle and a worse one using neuter qualifying words.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"In the next sentence of the source text, the two original spirits are personified as a pair, each independent in thoughts, declarations, and actions, and an admonition is given to choose the better one.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"These two spirits are said to have come together by natural combination to produce opposing phenomena such as life and its absence, and Heaven and Hell.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"Hell is described as “the worst life,” and Heaven as “the best mental state,” rather than a cruel place for innocents or a superstitious paradise.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"The commentator notes that the name Angra Mainyu does not occur in this section of the text.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"The dualistic creation is described as the proper Zarathustrian creation, abstract and limited, with the suggestion that many similar hymns likely existed beside Yasna XXX.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"The two original forces or beings are described as remaining clearly separate even when they come together; they do not blend unrecognizably.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:13","text":"After creating the two principles, each being chooses a particular realm: Ahura chooses the righteous order of religion and with it the pious of all ages, while the evil spirit chooses the wicked.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:14","text":"The doctrine is explained as maintaining that a good God cannot be responsible for permanent evil and that imperfection and suffering are original and inherent in the nature of things.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:15","text":"It is stated that the swallowing up of sin and sorrow in ultimate happiness belongs to a later period and is not part of Gathic Zarathustrianism.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:16","text":"Evil, including base and revolting moral qualities and their attendant miseries, is attributed to the work of an independent being described as an evil God.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:17","text":"Blood‑feuds of war and theological animosity are said to have been too much for the sage’s philosophy, preventing him from With a Baresman and the libation Zaothra, the speaker approaches the Myazda-offering, Ameretatai (guardian of plants and wood), Haurvatai (guardian of water), and fresh meat or milk to propitiate Ahura Mazda, the Bountiful Immortals, and Sraosha (Obedience), who is said to grant victory and advance settlements. The worshipper also approaches Haoma and Parahaoma for the propitiation of the Fravashi of the saint Spitama Zarathustra, and offers sacred wood with perfume to the Fire, addressed as the son of Ahura Mazda. Further, the Haomas, Haoma-water, fresh milk, and the plant Hadhanaepata are offered with sanctity for the Mazda-made waters. Finally, the worshipper approaches the Baresman with Zaothra again, along with thoughts well thought, words well spoken, deeds well done, the recital of the Gathas, the well-said Mathras, the (higher) content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.zoroastrian-avesta-yasna-gathas-mills-archive-l9509-l9606","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/zoroastrian/project-gutenberg/zend-avesta-part-3-yasna-gathas.md","passage_locator":{"label":"I42  THE    GATHAS. / YASNA    XLVI.  143 / YASNA    XLVII.  I45 / YASNA    XLVII.  I47; lines 9509-9606","start":"9509","end":"9606","translation":"The Zend-Avesta, Part III: The Yasna, Visparad, Afrinagan, Gahs, and Miscellaneous Fragments","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"“And to this (man, His chosen saint), Ahura Mazda will give both the two (greatest gifts, His) Universal Weal and Immortality… Aye, (that blessedness, which is the) best (creation) of this most bounteous spirit, Ahura Mazda will bring forth in action with words from the mouth and tongue of His Good Mind… And… Thou art He who for this (man… ) hath made the joy-creating Kine.”","summary":"The passage explains that Ahura Mazda will ultimately set all things right, granting the righteous a full share of the best goods while the faithless and wicked enjoy their wealth in a marred way apart from God. These divine gifts, including Universal Weal and Immortality, are mediated by Ahura Mazda’s bountiful Spirit, Good/Best Mind, Righteous Order, Sovereign Power established in Piety, and by His Fire. Piety (Aramaiti) and Good Mind are personified as instructive powers whose light converts those who come to them, leading all living beings to choose and believe in God; Ahura Mazda is also said to have created a joy‑giving Kine for the inspired man.","language":"English","quote_policy":"quoted"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"Ahura Mazda is described as ultimately setting all things right and giving the ashavan (righteous person) fullness, not a meagre share, of whatever is best.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1","ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"The dregvant and aka (faithless and wicked), though they may be prosperous, only taste the enjoyment of their wealth apart from God, and this enjoyment is said to be marred.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"The wicked are said to live in actions inspired not by the bountiful spirit but by the Evil Mind, whose mind is described as ‘aka’ (bad).","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"God’s gifts, including all that is best, are said to be given in connection with His Fire, which is imparted to the two struggling sides, the believing and the faithless.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"The passage explicitly speaks of two ‘struggling sides’: the believing and the faithless.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"Piety is described as an instructress who converts all those who come to her and seek her light.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"Piety is said to cause all the living to choose and believe in God.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"Ahura Mazda is said to give to ‘this man, His chosen saint’ the two greatest gifts: Universal Weal and Immortality.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"These gifts are given by means of Ahura Mazda’s bountiful Spirit, His Best Mind, His Righteous moral Order in word and deed, and His Sovereign Power established in Piety among His folk.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"Universal Weal and Immortality are identified as the ‘best’ or supreme goods, described as the best creation of the most bounteous spirit.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:3","ev:4","ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"Ahura Mazda will bring forth this best blessedness in action through words from the mouth and tongue of His Good Mind within His seers, and through the ‘two hands’ of Aramaiti (Piety) within the soul.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:4","ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"By such beneficence Ahura Mazda is called the father of the righteous Order within worship and life.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:13","text":"Ahura Mazda is described as the bountiful One who possesses the bounteous spirit and who has made the joy‑creating Kine for the man in whom this spirit works.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:14","text":"The Kine is elsewhere mentioned as uttering her wail, being answered by her maker, and taking counsel, indicating that she is treated as a speaking, counsel‑taking being.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:15","text":"The commentator notes an explicit personification of both Vohu Manah (Good Mind) and Aramaiti (Piety).","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]}],"figures":[{"id":"fig:1","name_or_label":"Ahura Mazda","description":"Supreme deity described as bountiful, possessor of the bountiful spirit, giver of Universal Weal and Immortality, father of righteous Order, and creator of the joy‑creating Kine, who grants gifts in connection with His Fire.","role_refs":["role:1","role:2"],"evidence_refs":["ev:1","ev:2","ev:3","ev:4","ev:5"]},{"id":"fig:2","name_or_label":"Ashavan / chosen saint","description":"The righteous person, referred to as ‘this man, His chosen saint’ and as ashavan, who receives Universal Weal, Immortality, and fullness of the best gifts from Ahura Mazda.","role_refs":["role:3"],"evidence_refs":["ev:1","ev:3"]},{"id":"fig:3","name_or_label":"Dregvant and aka (faithless and wicked people)","description":"A class of people described as faithless content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.zoroastrian-avesta-yasna-gathas-mills-archive-l10506-l10552","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/zoroastrian/project-gutenberg/zend-avesta-part-3-yasna-gathas.md","passage_locator":{"label":"I  62  THE    GATHAS. / YASNA    XLIX.  I  6 / YASNA    XLIX.  165 / YASNA   XLIX.  167; lines 10506-10552","start":"10506","end":"10552","translation":"The Zend-Avesta, Part III: The Yasna, Visparad, Afrinagan, Gahs, and Miscellaneous Fragments","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"\"the souls (of the evil dead) shall meet those evil men ... and in the Lie's abode their dwelling verily shall be\"","summary":"A Gathic verse describes worshippers entrusting their self-humbling praises to the deity's Good Mind, which protects the living and the spirits of the dead; these praises sustain Aramaiti (Piety) and sacrificing zeal and are offered to further the deity's great Sovereign Power with undying strength. The next verse depicts faithless reprobates whose souls meet those of the evil dead in hell, where they are welcomed with evil food and dwell in the Lie's abode. Editorial notes discuss conjectural wording, the role of Pahlavi translators, a suggested later identification of Vohu Manah with a faithful disciple, a parallel to the \"evil food\" motif in Yast XXII, and the significance of a verse naming Zarathustra for debates over authorship.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"The speaker entrusts self-humbling praises to the deity's Good Mind, which is invoked as protection for the living and for the spirits of the dead.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"Aramaiti is described as \"our Piety\" and is said to exist by means of the praises offered, along with sacrificing zeal.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"The worshippers say that their praises and sacrificing zeal are performed to further the deity's great Sovereign Power among the deity's folk, with \"undying\" strength.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1","ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"Faithless reprobates are described: the souls of the evil dead will meet evil men who served evil rulers, spoke evil words, and harboured evil consciences.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"The souls in hell will come with evil food to welcome these evil men, and their dwelling will be in the Lie's abode.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"A note suggests that this description of the Good Mind may underlie a later identification of Vohu Manah with the faithful disciple.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"The commentator explains that the adjective rendered \"undying\" is conjectural and based on Pahlavi evidence, noting alternative understandings about those who think upon the throne to seize it with dying power.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"The commentator states that Pahlavi translators seldom deliberately guessed, instead reworking the shattered results of their predecessors and re-delivering what they heard and read.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:4","ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"A note on the \"evil food\" refers the reader to Yast XXII as content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.zoroastrian-avesta-yasna-gathas-mills-archive-l6722-l6806","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/zoroastrian/project-gutenberg/zend-avesta-part-3-yasna-gathas.md","passage_locator":{"label":"YASNA    XXXIV.  87 / YASNA    XXXIV.  89 / YASNA   XLIII.  91 / THE    GATHA(A)    U-STAVAITI(I).; lines 6722-6806","start":"6722","end":"6806","translation":"The Zend-Avesta, Part III: The Yasna, Visparad, Afrinagan, Gahs, and Miscellaneous Fragments","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"This editorial passage introduces the Ustavaiti Gatha (Yasna XLIII–XLVI). Mills explains that the Gatha is named from its opening word and treated as a unit because of its particular metre, but that metre and manuscript ordering do not reliably indicate the relative age of the Gathas; only their contents do. He then characterizes Yasna XLVI as depicting Zarathustra before he attained his supreme position: Zarathustra laments the poor prospects of his cause, feels vehement animosity, urges his adherents to overthrow a powerful opposing leader, anticipates a formidable armed struggle whose partisans are elsewhere called \"hosts,\" and exhorts the chiefs of his party as they stand before him in a large assembly, possibly an army before an important encounter. In this context he refers closely to the monarch, to his own family (the Spitamas), and to the Hvogva clan represented by Frashaartra, offering Ahura’s rewards along with threats and condemnations. Mills notes that similarly intense passages of grief, fear, and resentment occur throughout the Gathas and likely belong to Zarathustra’s earlier career, while he tentatively suggests that chapters XXIX (on sufferings to be remedied and Zarathustra’s call) and XXX (with theosophical statements) may have been composed in a later period of success and reflection. He adds that chapter LIII, celebrating the marriage of Zarathustra’s daughter, seems to come from Zarathustra’s mature but not necessarily advanced age, and concludes that the placement of a piece in a particular Gatha provides little evidence for its relative date.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"The Ustavaiti Gatha consists of Yasna chapters XLIII–XLVI and is named from the word that begins it.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"The existence of the Gatha as a unit is attributed to the nature of its metre, not to later associations with happy anticipations.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"The Gatha’s lines generally have eleven syllables arranged in stanzas of five, and hymns of one particular metre were chanted together.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"The order of the Gathas in the manuscripts of the Yasna may have been altered for liturgical purposes, and metre yields no clear indication of relative age.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"The metre of the Ustavaiti is said to approach the Trish/up, and the oldest ^shis are described as having sung in Trish/up.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"Mills asserts that the sole remaining test of the relative age of pieces is their contents and the circumstances they treat.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"Yasna XLVI is described as showing Zarathustra at a time before he had attained his supreme position.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"In this depiction, Zarathustra laments the unfavourable prospects of his cause and is full of vehement animosity.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"Zarathustra urges his adherents toward the overthrow of a powerful opposing leader and anticipates a formidable armed struggle whose partisans are elsewhere called \"hosts.\"","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"Zarathustra is portrayed as exhorting various chiefs of his party as they stand before him in a large assembly, possibly an army on the eve of an important encounter.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"In this context Zarathustra refers closely to the monarch, to his own family the Spitamas, and to the Hvogvas represented by Frashaartra.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"Zarathustra offers the rewards of Ahura and pronounces His threats and condemnations.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:13","text":"Mills considers these features of Yasna XLVI to bear strong evidence of originality.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:14","text":"Passages expressing grief, fear, and passionate resentment occur in several Gathas and are suggested to refer to Zarathustra personally and to the earlier portion of his career.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:15","text":"Chapter XXIX is described as logically commencing with content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.zoroastrian-avesta-yasna-gathas-mills-archive-l5092-l5196","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/zoroastrian/project-gutenberg/zend-avesta-part-3-yasna-gathas.md","passage_locator":{"label":"YASNA  XXXII. / YASNA   XXXII.  55 / YASNA    XXXII.  57 / YASNA    XXXII.  59; lines 5092-5196","start":"5092","end":"5196","translation":"The Zend-Avesta, Part III: The Yasna, Visparad, Afrinagan, Gahs, and Miscellaneous Fragments","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"This portion of Yasna XXXII describes the Demon-gods (Daevas) as beloved yet forsaken by the Good Mind and led far astray from the understanding of the Great Creator, the Living Lord, and His Righteousness. They, under the rule of the Evil Spirit and his evil mind, beguile mankind of happy life on earth and of immortality beyond it, with an evil word guiding wicked actions. A criminal leader among them desires to destroy the speaker and is famed for his doctrine. In contrast, Ahura is said to possess true teachings in His memory, together with His kingdom and Righteous Order. I  I  7; lines 8022-8120","start":"8022","end":"8120","translation":"The Zend-Avesta, Part III: The Yasna, Visparad, Afrinagan, Gahs, and Miscellaneous Fragments","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"In this portion of Yasna XLIV the speaker repeatedly addresses Ahura (Mazda), asking to be told \"aright\" who is truly righteous or evil and why a vile man who opposes him in gaining Ahura's blessing is not recognized as the sinner he is. He looks upon polluted worshippers with his spirit's hate. He then asks how to banish the Demon-of-the-Lie from among them down to rebellious beings beneath, lamenting that the friends of Righteousness, as it lives in Ahura's saints, gain no light from teachings and have not loved the questions posed by the Good Mind in the soul. The speaker further asks how to deliver this Demon-of-the-Lie into the two hands of Ahura's Order so she may be cast down to death through the Mathras (doctrinal formulas), bringing destruction among her evil believers and preventing deceitful, harsh oppressors from achieving their aims. Finally, he asks whether, through Righteousness within their souls, Ahura can protect him when two hostile hosts meet in hate over vows that Ahura desires to maintain, and to which party Ahura will grant victory, with verse 16 beginning another formulaic question whose content is not fully given in the excerpt.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"The speaker looks upon polluted worshippers with his spirit's hate.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"The speaker asks Ahura to tell him aright who is the righteous one in the matter about which he questions.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"The speaker asks who is evil, which person is wicked, and which is the foremost wicked one.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"The speaker refers to a vile man who stands against him in gaining Ahura's blessing and questions why this man is not regarded and believed to be the sinner he is.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"The speaker asks Ahura how to banish the Demon-of-the-Lie from among them to those beneath who are filled with rebellion.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"The speaker states that the friends of Righteousness, as it lives in Ahura's saints, gain no light from their teachings and have not loved the questions which the Good Mind asks in the soul.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"The speaker asks how to deliver the Demon-of-the-Lie into the two hands of Ahura's Order, so that she may be cast down to death through the Mathras of doctrine.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"The speaker seeks to send mighty destruction among the Demon-of-the-Lie's evil believers and to keep deceitful and harsh oppressors from attaining their aims.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"The speaker asks whether, through Righteousness within their souls, Ahura has power to Divine qualities such as the Good Mind, Aramaiti (Piety), Righteous Order, Universal Weal, and Immortality are personified as powers dwelling in Mazda’s Kingdom: they withdraw from the unjust, aid the faithful, and strike tyrants with fear. Aramaiti is said to increase Universal Weal and Immortality and to strengthen the righteous ritual and moral order. The speaker concludes by asking Mazda to reveal his regulations and the correct praise and offerings that will secure blessed rewards under his ordinance. Translator’s notes briefly associate the ‘food’ of Weal and Immortality with the Lord-of-water and Lord-of-wood, or simply ‘water and tree,’ in later Avesta and content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.zoroastrian-avesta-yasna-gathas-mills-archive-l6007-l6116","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/zoroastrian/project-gutenberg/zend-avesta-part-3-yasna-gathas.md","passage_locator":{"label":"YASNA    XXXIII.  71 / YASNA    XXXIII.  73 / YASNA    XXXIII.  75 / YASNA    XXXIII.  77; lines 6007-6116","start":"6007","end":"6116","translation":"The Zend-Avesta, Part III: The Yasna, Visparad, Afrinagan, Gahs, and Miscellaneous Fragments","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"In Yasna XXXIII (verses 10–13 in this section), a first-person worshipper prays to Ahura Mazda and a group of personified divine qualities—Aramaiti (piety), Righteous Order, Good Mind, Sovereign Power, and Sanctity—for prosperity, salvation, mercy, power, strength, and understanding. He asks for all prosperous states in past, present, and future to be granted in divine love and for bodily and personal life to be blessed with salvation through Good Mind, Sovereign Power, and Sanctity. He addresses Ahura Mazda and the other personified qualities, asking them all to hear him and have mercy on every deed. He then petitions Ahura to arise to him, to give him power through Aramaiti in response to his appeals and offerings, and to grant him mighty strength and the \"thrift-law\" through Good Mind. I  I  7 / YASNA   XLIV.  119 / YASNA    XLIV.  121 / YASNA  XLV.; lines 8269-8311","start":"8269","end":"8311","translation":"The Zend-Avesta, Part III: The Yasna, Visparad, Afrinagan, Gahs, and Miscellaneous Fragments","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"Scholarly commentary introduces Yasna XLV as a hymn titled \"The Doctrine of Dualism\" and an homage to Ahura. The hymn is said to resemble Yasna XXX and to come from a time of political calm and theological activity, following the crushing of a powerful adversary identified with the dujsasti of Y. XXXII, 9. An assembly from near and far, likely the victorious side, is addressed in a congratulatory tone. The hymn is presented as meant for a large crowd, summoned with escalating calls to \"awake your ears,\" \"listen,\" and \"ponder.\" The evil teacher Antizarathmtra is described as having been defeated so that he can no longer disturb the community or preach beside the orthodox preachers. The speaker then reiterates the central doctrine contested in the conflict: social evils do not originate from, nor are they tolerated by, the holy Ahura, but instead arise from the personified Anger of the Daevas—the evil Mainyu, the Angra (angry) Spirit. A fixed gulf is said to separate this evil being from Ahura, whose purity is never compromised by complicity in cruelty or evil passions. The commentator notes that the defeated dujsasti may possibly have been a Daeva-worshipper and thus a heretic from this faith.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"Yasna XLV is introduced under the heading \"The Doctrine of Dualism. Homage to Ahura.\"","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"The hymn of Yasna XLV is said to recall Yasna XXX and to belong to a period of political repose and theological activity, with a smoother and more continuous style than usual.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"A powerful adversary is described as having just been crushed, identified as the dujsasti of Yasna XXXII, 9.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"An assembly is addressed, as in Yasna XXX, 1, but this time the assembly is described \"listen\" (sraota), and \"ponder\" (mazdaunghodum).","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"Antizarathmtra is called \"the evil teacher par eminence\" and is said to have preachers.\"","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"The commentary states that the speaker then reiterates the chief doctrine over which the parties had been at war, There is discussion of the shift between first- and third-person speech, the uncertain authorship of these verses (whether Zarathushtra or another composer), and example phrases such as 'I approach,' 'I offer,' 'he will act,' and 'let him be in Asha's pastures.' The commentary then explains that the strictest canon for both original and later Zoroastrians was a 'primeval law' derived from a dualistic principle that forbids any compromise with evil, especially foreign creeds. Ahura is said to have no share in corruption and no power to prevent sin or sorrow, though full power to oppose them. Within this framework the Ratu acts with severity toward evil and beneficence toward the saint, and fierce hostilities against the wicked are declared more than justified: harming the wicked through denunciation, planning, or physical violence is equated with advising the good, and pursuing Ahura's enemies is described as an act of love toward God and a sacrifice to religion itself.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"The commentary states that brighter times seem to have arrived and that the vengeance promised at the close of Yasna XXXII is described as near at hand.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"The first three verses of Yasna XXXIII are said to belong as much to Finally, he asks what sentence will fall upon the recreant who withholds this honoured gift from the deserving veracious tiller of the earth and correct speaker of the sacrificial word, who shows no It explains that the prophet proclaims an absolute separation between good and evil, God and Demon, expressed as two opposing spirits that made life and its negation and remain in irreconcilable opposition. The sage claims to declare the first Mathra revealed by all‑wise Mazda, warning that those who do not act in accordance with it will end life in woe, while those who listen and ponder it gain Happiness and Immortality. The commentary then dwells on the fatherhood of God, describing Mazda as this world's best being, father of the Good Mind within His people and of practical piety as His daughter, requiring a ready and undeceivable servant's mind. It continues that Ahura, through His Good Mind and Immortal Archangels present in the believer's soul, rewards listeners. The prophet finally designates praise (including prayer and doctrinal confession) as the greatest element, linked to spiritual blessings sought by living offerers, future generations, and the spirits of the just in eternal Immortality, where a divine law brings woe to the wicked. Zarathustra (or his substitute) expresses eagerness to serve Ahura with these greatest words, having \"seen\" Him through Righteous Order in his soul, and hopes to praise Him both in the assembly and in the 'Home of sublimity or song.'","language":"English","quote_policy":"quoted"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"A figure is described as a recreant or self‑styled Mazda‑worshipper who may have claimed rightful allegiance to the urvata and to the future blessings and temporal advantages of correct discipleship while using the name of the sacred tenets of the Religion to promote a nefarious warfare, and who is regarded by genuine adherents as effectively a Daeva‑worshipper.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"The commentary distinguishes this self‑styled Mazda‑worshipper from those \"of Zarathustra's order,\" saying he is not owned by genuine adherents and is met as a real, if not open, Daeva‑worshipper.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"The prophet is said to declare \"the utter severance between the good and the evil, the God and the Demon.\"","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"Two spirits are described as having come together at first to make life and its negation, co‑operating in an irreconcilable antagonism whose antitheses and friction make sentient existence possible; their union consists in opposition, and if they were to blend they would cease to be what they are, so they remain forever separate in every attribute and interest.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:2","ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"The sage asserts that he is proclaiming the first Mathra of this life, which the all‑wise Mazda had revealed to him.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"He teaches that those who do not act in a manner accordant with what he speaks and even thinks, having previously announced it, are delinquents for whom this life should end in woe.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"The commentary says he proceeds to dwell on the fatherhood of God, declaring that this world's best being is Mazda Himself.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"Ahura Mazda is described as metaphorically called His daughter, while pretended good intention and idle sentiment are denied any relationship with Him.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"God is said to need a 'ready mind' within His servant and is declared not to be deceived.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"Returning to the Mathra, the commentary states that Happiness and Immortality would be the portion of those who listened to and pondered the revelation.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"Ahura Himself is described as approaching such listeners with the rewarding actions of His Good Mind and as being in all good actions.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:13","text":"Ahura's Immortal Archangels are said to have their objective existence in the believer's soul.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:14","text":"Turning from admonition to worship, the prophet announces the 'greatest' element, namely praise which includes both prayer and doctrinal confessions, and he calls on Ahura both to listen and to teach.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:15","text":"These spiritual blessings are Immortality.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:16","text":"According to a well‑remembered law, the blessings include 'woe to the wicked,' arising not only from outward discipline but also from inward grief.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:17","text":"Ahura is said to have established beneficent but solemn regulations regarding these outcomes by exercising His Sovereign Power as controller of all.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:18","text":"Zarathustra (or his substitute) professes eagerness to serve She is given a choice between an earth-tilling husbandman and one who is not a tiller; she chooses the thrifty husbandman as a holy master endowed with the Good Mind’s wealth. The thieving nomad is said never to share the good creed, which the Kine’s choice would otherwise bestow. Translator’s notes explain that cattle here symbolize civic life, that the path is the religious ‘way’ for the people, and that the husbandman is identified in later Avesta with Zarathustra. The passage then recalls that this doctrine of the Kine’s choice was a first rule to regulate actions. Ahura Mazda is praised as creator of holy settlements and revealer of religious laws, giver of understanding from his own mind and of bodily life, and as the one who delivers injunctions so that a ‘wisher’ may place his choices. A Pahlavi gloss adds that even the desire for the other world and what is needed upon arrival there are granted by God, and interprets the final line as referring to religious preferences and moral volition. The text notes that strife arose and still rages: beside God’s prophet, a person—whether truthful or lying, enlightened or unenlightened—lifts his voice. Commentary describes the exclusion of the nomad from the good creed as a kind of judicial blindness in which the wicked are kept from seeing the He prays to be taught the great thoughts or salvation-schemes of the Saviours—the khratu of life—who through conflict and reverses will eventually bring about ‘Completed Progress.’ Rousing himself from grief, he calls for a reward for a chief who, with his retainers, will expel the world-destroyer (dujsasti) from power and life, with the reward described as recognition and confirmation of merit He singles out punishment for those who install an evil monarch of the Daeva-party who persecutes a pious husbandman opposing the Lie-demon. The speaker asks how a wise man may become like Ahura, contrasts disciples of Asha (Righteous Order) with their opponents allied to the harmful Lie, and prays not to be misled by blind guides but to be instructed by the enlightened, even by Ahura Himself. He warns his congregation not to heed the opponents’ doctrines, associating them with ruin and death and even appealing to the sword. He then prays that they may listen to Ahura, who can vindicate the conscientious Zarathurtrian and encourage truthfulness by means of a holy sacrifice or ordeal of Fire. Those who seduce the righteous are warned that their self-induced sorrows and their own consciences will form part of their punishment, whereas the faithful will receive happiness and immortality, together with Righteousness and the Good and Kindly Mind. I  I  I; lines 7711-7809","start":"7711","end":"7809","translation":"The Zend-Avesta, Part III: The Yasna, Visparad, Afrinagan, Gahs, and Miscellaneous Fragments","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"“This I ask Thee, O Ahura! tell me aright; when praise is to be offered, how shall I complete the praise of the One like You, O Mazda?”","summary":"The commentary and translation discuss a section of Yasna XLIV. The commentator explains that the speaker invokes the Mind of Ahura as a hoped-for champion Ratu, hints that he himself may be this coming leader, seeks a closer conference with Ahura through revelation so he can protect the people and secure the abiding gifts of Weal and Immortality. He asks for an honorary gift of mares and a camel to be used as sacrificial material, probably before battle, for the people’s lasting welfare, and warns that any monarch who withholds this aid will face instant judgment. The peroration appeals to wavering groups to recognize evil as evil, denounces the Daevas and their adherents as violent, unjust rulers, and describes the Kine, representing sacred herds and people, crying out. The commentator describes verses 12–20 as a religious war-song later joined to calmer verses 1–10 and closely connected with Yasna XLVI. The translated verses then show the speaker asking Ahura how to complete proper praise, requesting that the ‘One like Thee’ instruct a friend like him so that, through Righteousness and the Good Mind within, divine help and nearness may be gained. A second verse asks how to serve the supreme one of Heaven, the better world, who grants blessings and seeks grateful response, and portrays Mazda as bountiful through the Righteous Order, holding off content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.zoroastrian-avesta-yasna-gathas-mills-archive-l2923-l3020","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/zoroastrian/project-gutenberg/zend-avesta-part-3-yasna-gathas.md","passage_locator":{"label":"YASNA  XXVIII. / YASNA    XXVIII.  15 / I  6  THE    GATHAS. / YASNA    XXVIII.  17; lines 2923-3020","start":"2923","end":"3020","translation":"The Zend-Avesta, Part III: The Yasna, Visparad, Afrinagan, Gahs, and Miscellaneous Fragments","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"\"With venerating desire for this gift of gracious help, O Mazda, and stretching forth my hands to Thee I pray ... that my actions toward all may be performed in the Divine Righteousness; and with this I implore from Thee the understanding of Thy Benevolent Mind, in order that I may propitiate the Soul of the Kine (our herds and folk, which cries so bitterly to Thee).\"","summary":"The passage opens with a liturgical blessing that declares Zarathustra's thought, word, and deed to be blessings, invokes the Bountiful Immortals to accept and support the chants, and pays homage to the sacred Gathas. It then presents a first-person prayer to Mazda in which the speaker, stretching out hands in veneration, asks that all actions be carried out in Divine Righteousness, implores understanding from Mazda's Benevolent Mind to propitiate the Soul of the Kine (identified with the suffering herds and folk), and, inspired by that Benevolent Mind, approaches the Great Creator and Living Lord to request attainments in both the corporeal world and the world of mind, derived from Divine Righteousness, so that this personified Righteousness may introduce its recipients into beatitude and glory. Translator notes expand on Mazda as the most bounteous Spirit (likened to the Holy Spirit in Semitic scriptures) and discuss the rendering of terms related to heavenly beatitude.","language":"English","quote_policy":"quoted"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"Zarathustra's thought, word, and deed are each described as a blessing.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"The Bountiful Immortals are asked to accept and help on the chants.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"The sacred Gathas are directly addressed with homage.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"The speaker stretches forth his or her hands toward Mazda while praying for the first blessing of the bountiful Spirit.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"The speaker prays that his or her actions toward all may be performed in the Divine Righteousness.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"The speaker implores Mazda for the understanding of His Benevolent Mind.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"The purpose of gaining understanding is to propitiate the Soul of the Kine, glossed as the herds and folk that cry bitterly to Mazda.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"The speaker, inspired by the Benevolent Mind, approaches the addressed deity or deities to request further gifts.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"The requested gift is attainments for both the corporeal world and the world of mind, derived from Divine Righteousness.","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"Personified Divine Righteousness within humans is said to be able to introduce those who receive it into beatitude and glory.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"Mazda is described as the Great Creator and Living Lord, and elsewhere as the most bounteous Spirit, whose bountifulness is understood as gracious, sacred, and august.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:3","ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"The translator compares the usage of 'bounteous Spirit' in the Avesta to the Holy Spirit in Semitic scriptures, where the Spirit is both God and 'of God.'","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:13","text":"The translator prefers to render the goal state as 'glorious beatitude' and rejects translations like 'comfortable stone heaven' or 'delectable mountains' as unlikely in the Avesta context.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]}],"figures":[{"id":"fig:1","name_or_label":"Zarathustra","description":"A righteous figure whose thought, word, and deed are each described as a blessing.","role_refs":["role:1"],"evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"fig:2","name_or_label":"Bountiful Immortals (Ameshospends)","description":"A collective of divine beings called the Bountiful Immortals, identified with the Ameshospends, who are invoked to accept and support the chants.","role_refs":["role:2"],"evidence_refs":["ev:1","ev:6"]},{"id":"fig:3","name_or_label":"Sacred veneration.","role_refs":["role:3"],"evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"fig:4","name_or_label":"Mazda / Ahura, the Great Creator","description":"The deity addressed as Mazda, described as the Great kingdom.","role_refs":["role:4"],"evidence_refs":["ev:2","ev:3","ev:4"]},{"id":"fig:5","name_or_label":"Benevolent Mind","description":"Mazda's Benevolent Mind, from which understanding is sought and content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.zoroastrian-avesta-yasna-gathas-mills-archive-l6907-l6987","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/zoroastrian/project-gutenberg/zend-avesta-part-3-yasna-gathas.md","passage_locator":{"label":"THE    GATHA(A)    U-STAVAITI(I). / YASNA    XLIII.  93 / YASNA   XLIII. / YASNA    XLIII.  95; lines 6907-6987","start":"6907","end":"6987","translation":"The Zend-Avesta, Part III: The Yasna, Visparad, Afrinagan, Gahs, and Miscellaneous Fragments","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"Mills’ prose commentary on Yasna XLIII.95 describes how the seer begins praising Ahura as all-bountiful, nurturing means of grace that teach moral sanctity. These gifts include holy Fire, which rallied the people to national worship and supported the holy order. Through these means, the Good Mind of Ahura strengthens the seer. The commentator says that, like a Semitic prophet, the seer poetically imagines himself beholding Ahura as chief of the two spirits at the world’s birth, when Ahura established rewards and punishments, which will fully issue at the “last turning of the creation.” The seer fervently prays for Ahura’s coming in this last change and for the Sacred Kingdom, guarded by divine Benevolence, to appear when settlements are furthered in the Righteous Order. In that consummation, the piety of souls will themselves instruct, giving regulations that end the controversy of two sides; these are identified with the penetrating wisdom of Ahura’s understanding that lays bare all thoughts. The passage then explains the principles by which the seer accepted the divine call: Sraosha (Obedience), the way to Ahura and the angel of the Deity, draws near as his personified conscience and loyalty, representing the obedient people, to question him about his origin and course. Speaking in Zarathustra’s name, the seer declares an uncompromising path: unbelieving opposers will receive no favour but detestation, while devout disciples will receive strong aid. His mind is fixed on the ideal Kingdom as he labours to prepare for Frashakart and composes hymns as the “machinery of lore.” The conscience/obedient will then questions him again, offering religious knowledge, and the seer mentions holy Fire with its proper offering as the first subject of inquiry.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"The composer begins ascriptions of praise by regarding Ahura as all-bountiful and mighty, who has nurtured aids of grace to bestow on humans.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"Ahura’s aids of grace are described as gifts of forbearance, extended even to those now wicked in hope of their penitence through a merciful threat of punishment, and as benefits to a devout disciple whose piety is not merely ceremonial.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"These means of grace are said to abound in inculcating moral sanctity in thought, word, and deed, and are explicitly noted as not being limited to ritual meaning.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"Aside from the flame of the holy Fire, the means of grace are called profane; the holy Fire is credited with rallying the masses to a national worship and with being strong for the holy order.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"The might of the Good Mind of Ahura is described as approaching the seer through these gifts of grace and giving him strength for all that lay before him.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"The commentator states that, like a Semitic prophet, the seer poetically conceives himself as having beheld Ahura as chief of the two spirits and sovereign over all other powers when the world was born.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"Ahura is regarded as having established rewards and punishments at the birth of the world by his holiness, which is sharply distinguished in dualistic fashion from any complicity with evil whether by infliction or permission.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"These rewards and punishments are said to have their issue not in time alone, but also in “the last turning of the creation” in its course.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"The seer fervently beseeches Ahura to come in this last changing and also for the appearance of a Sacred Kingdom established and guarded by divine Benevolence.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"The consummation is described as occurring when settlements have been furthered in the Righteous Order, after which the piety of men’s souls will itself be their instructor, delivering regulations that will silence the controversy of the two sides.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"These future regulations are equated with the wisdom of Ahura’s understanding, which is said to be so penetrating that all thoughts lie bare to it.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"The seer explains that Sraosha, called Obedience and the way to Ahura, is described as drawing near to question him as he accepts the divine call, representing his obedient spirit listening to God.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:13","text":"The personified conscience identified with Sraosha is said to represent the obedient people as well as the obedient sage; it is glossed as “Loyalty” that questions the seer so that loyalty may report his answers.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:14","text":"Speaking in the name of Zarathustra, or someone thoroughly in unison with him, the seer states that his course will aid.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:15","text":"The seer’s mind and thought are said to be fixed on the ideal Kingdom, and meanwhile he continues to toil, making content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.zoroastrian-avesta-yasna-gathas-mills-archive-l8760-l8812","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/zoroastrian/project-gutenberg/zend-avesta-part-3-yasna-gathas.md","passage_locator":{"label":"YASNA    XLV.  127 / YASNA    XLV.  129 / YASNA    XLVI.  I3I / I32  THE    GAT  HAS.; lines 8760-8812","start":"8760","end":"8812","translation":"The Zend-Avesta, Part III: The Yasna, Visparad, Afrinagan, Gahs, and Miscellaneous Fragments","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"The passage comments on instructions and prayers in the Gathas. Whoever expels or destroys a heretical tyrant will be highly esteemed for supporting the people and their sacred agricultural civilisation, but this prestige is itself to be offered back to God for further service. Every righteous official must repeatedly proclaim a warning to polluted Daeva‑worshippers and secret adherents, and after careful discrimination is to confront the evil chief or hostile kinsman, informing him of the price on his head. A superintendent who has power yet fails to carry out these commands will be bound to the Lie‑demon served by the evil kinsman. The text asserts there is no compromise in a dualistic moral creed: one who favours evil is counted as evil, and the friend of good is as good, as ordained by the Lord. The speaker turns to the sacramental Fire as an outward emblem of inward grace that aids the masses in worship and asks who has been set as his strengthener in storms besides God and His symbolic flames, mentioning Good Mind and Order with them. He prays that anyone who would destroy his settlement will find all forces turned toward his ruin and be kept from prosperity but not from harm. He then calls for a leading helper to magnify Ahura and advance the sacred cause following Ahura’s conciliation. To encourage his listeners, he vows never to abandon the faithful few but to accompany them even to the dread assize, helping them through the final test. By contrast, the wicked, whether open or concealed, will not share these hopes; their conscience, described as a remorseless executioner, will curse them as they attempt to cross the Judgment Bridge.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"Whoever expels or destroys the heretical tyrant will be highly recognised for supporting the people and their sacred agricultural civilisation.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"The prestige or eminence gained by defending the people is considered sufficient reward and is to be given back to God as an offering for further service.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"Every righteous official is urged to repeat a proclamation as a warning to polluted Daeva‑worshippers and to secret adherents.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"The charged official is instructed to assail the destructive opponent only after careful discrimination, approaching the evil chief or hostile kinsman rather than the inferior noble or peasant clansman.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"The official is to tell the evil chief fully about the price set on his head.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"A superintendent who has the power but does not carry out these instructions will be delivered over to the bonds of the Lie‑demon whom the evil kinsman serves.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"The text states there is no compromise in a dualistic moral creed: the man who favours the evil is as the evil, and the friend of the good is as the good himself, as ordained by the Lord.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"The speaker turns his Editorial notes discuss whether the reward is positive or retributive, explain that Vayu has two natures and can be invoked in good or evil senses, and compare the foiling and delivering of evil here content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.zoroastrian-avesta-yasna-gathas-mills-archive-l9412-l9506","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/zoroastrian/project-gutenberg/zend-avesta-part-3-yasna-gathas.md","passage_locator":{"label":"YASNA    XLVI.  14I / I42  THE    GATHAS. / YASNA    XLVI.  143 / YASNA    XLVII.  I45; lines 9412-9506","start":"9412","end":"9506","translation":"The Zend-Avesta, Part III: The Yasna, Visparad, Afrinagan, Gahs, and Miscellaneous Fragments","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"Mills introduces the Spenta Mainyu Gatha (Yasna XLVII–L), noting its metrical structure and that only fragments may survive. He explains that in Yasna XLVII the Spenta Mainyu is Ahura’s indwelling Spirit, distinct from Ahura, and discusses how the term 'spenta' applied to a group of seven beings (the Amesha Spentas) may have inspired later ideas of 'seven spirits before the throne of God', though he denies a direct link to the Christian 'Holy Spirit'. Through this Spirit, Ahura bestows on the 'ideal saint' the twin gift of comprehensive Happiness and its continuation in Immortality, not directly but via personified attributes: Benevolence or Best Mind, a plan of Order and Purity (Asha), Royal Power as the archangel Khshathra embodied in the sacred state, and practical Piety (Aramaiti), described as Ahura’s daughter. The composer prays that Ahura’s holy scheme will be carried out by domestic piety and by the spoken words of Good Mind from faithful priests, so that Ahura becomes Father of Asha, the divine Order, and of moral and ritual regularity among humans. The Spirit is further described as Ahura’s own bounteous Spirit, through whom he created the sacred symbolic Kine, emblem and substance of joy and representation of the holy people and their possessions, and in response to her wail arranged meadows 'of Piety' for her. The same Spirit vindicates Mazda’s justice by afflicting the wicked with a 'long wounding' for their sins and for preferring prosperous men of bad, dishonest, and heretical character.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"The Spenta Mainyu Gatha consists of Yasna XLVII–L and is named from its opening words; its metre has eleven-syllable lines arranged in stanzas of four, described as Trishtup-like.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"The grouping of hymns in this Gatha is said to have little or nothing to do with their relative age, and only fragments of a more extended piece may survive.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"The commentator notes signs of authorship apart from Zarathustra, but considers the later verses close in time to the Zarathustrian verses.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"Spenta Mainyu ('Spewta mainyu') is described as not identical with Ahura but as his Spirit, often referred to as his indwelling, blessed Spirit.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"The term 'spenta' applied to 'the seven' gives the Amesha Spentas (Amshaspands), and all seven are said to be deliberately grouped in the first verse, though 'His Spirit' is not one of them.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"The term 'spenta' forms the basis of a play on words in the later epilogue Visparad XIX, according to the commentator.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"The commentary states that Ahura’s indwelling Spirit gives the designation 'spirit' to the Amesha Spentas and may have been the original of the 'seven spirits which are before the throne of God', while having probably no direct connection with the 'Holy Spirit' of the Old and New Testaments.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"By means of his indwelling Spirit, in accordance with his inmost thoughts, Ahura bestows a gift upon the 'ideal saint', described as one who works the best results for Zarathustra, the Ratu, and the prophet.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"The gift bestowed on the ideal saint is said to be the 'inseparable two': Happiness in every particular, and the prospect and realization of the continuance of that Happiness in Immortality.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"Ahura is said not to bestow this gift by his immediate action, which humans could not apprehend unaided, but through his revealed Benevolence or Best Mind, his plan of Order and Purity, his Royal Power as 'archangel' Khshathra embodied in the sacred state, and practical piety called Aramaiti, described as his daughter and 'the ready mind'.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"The revelation of these component parts of the divine mind and will is described as simple enough for the labouring classes to understand initially, but later overgrown with 'weeds of superstition and myth'.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"The composer prays that Ahura may carry out his holy scheme into action by the 'busy hands and fingers' of domestic piety and by the preached and recited words of the Good Mind from the mouths and tongues of faithful priests.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:13","text":"The commentator says that only through domestic piety and the priests’ proclamation of the Good Mind would Ahura become the Father of Asha, the divine Order, and of moral and ritual regularity among men.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:14","text":"The exposition moves from discourse about God to an address to him, identifying the Spirit mentioned earlier as Ahura’s own and calling Ahura the bountiful one.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:15","text":"Ahura is described as the one who created the sacred symbolic Kine, which is both the emblem and substance of 'joy' and represents the possessions of the holy people and the people themselves.","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:16","text":"In response to the Kine’s wail mentioned elsewhere, Ahura has spread for her the meadows 'of Piety', arranged in consultations made on her behalf.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:17","text":"The Spirit is said not to confine itself to inspiring Piety alone but also to vindicate Mazda’s justice by afflicting the wicked with a 'long wounding' for their sins.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:18","text":"The wicked are punished not only for their sins but also for their cynical preference for prosperous men of bad and dishonest character and of heretical faith.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]}],"figures":[{"id":"fig:1","name_or_label":"Ahura / Mazda","description":"Bountiful supreme deity whose indwelling Spirit acts in the world; creator of the sacred symbolic Kine, bestower of happiness and immortality, vindicator of justice, and described as becoming Father of Asha and of moral and ritual prophet'.","role_refs":["role:10"],"evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"fig:6","name_or_label":"Ideal saint","description":"The exemplary righteous person on whom Ahura, through his Spirit, bestows the content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.zoroastrian-avesta-yasna-gathas-mills-archive-l12024-l12069","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/zoroastrian/project-gutenberg/zend-avesta-part-3-yasna-gathas.md","passage_locator":{"label":"THE    YASNA. / YASNA  I. / YASNA    I.  197 / I98  YASNA    I.; lines 12024-12069","start":"12024","end":"12069","translation":"The Zend-Avesta, Part III: The Yasna, Visparad, Afrinagan, Gahs, and Miscellaneous Fragments","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"A liturgical speaker declares that he \"announces\" and \"completes\" his Yasna (ritual) in honor of various beings and sacred times. He dedicates it to a victory-bringing figure who furthers the settlements, to Rashnu \"the most just\" and to Arstal who advances and increases the settlements. He then dedicates the Yasna to Mahya, the monthly festivals, described as lords of the ritual order; to the new and later moons, called holy lords of the ritual order; and to the full moon that scatters night. The speaker continues by dedicating the Yasna to Yairya, the yearly feasts, and to a series of named festivals (Maidyo-zaremya, Maidyo-shema, Paiti^hahya, Ayathrima, Maidhyairya, Hamaspathmaedhaya), all labeled holy lords of the ritual order, and finally to the seasons themselves. He concludes by announcing and completing the Yasna to all \"thirty and three\" lords of the ritual order who are said to be closest and around Havani. Editorial notes gloss Rashnu and Arstal as forms of rectitude, explain some festival names and the phrase for the \"later\" moon, interpret Ayathrima as belonging to the rutting season, and remark on the striking coincidence between this group of thirty-three lords and the Indian tradition of thirty-three gods in several Vedic and epic texts, though the names differ.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"The speaker announces and completes the Yasna to a figure described as one \"who smites with victory, and furthers the settlements.\"","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"Rashnu is named as \"the most just\" and is glossed in a footnote as a \"Genius of rectitude.\"","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:1","ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"Arstal is invoked after Rashnu and is said to \"advance the settlements\" and \"cause them to increase,\" and a footnote glosses Arstal as \"Rectitude in another form.\"","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:1","ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"Mahya is identified as the monthly festivals and is described as lords of the ritual order, to whom the speaker announces and completes his Yasna.","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"The new and the later moon are invoked as a holy lord of the ritual order, and the later moon is glossed as \"the moon within,\" showing little light.","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:2","ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"The full moon is described as \"which scatters night\" and is included among the recipients of the Yasna.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"The Yairya, yearly feasts, The sacred Kine is said to be all in all to the pious worshipper, representing all wealth in herds and sustaining the home-life of happy industry, with Ahura causing herbage to grow for her support. Order.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"Havani, Savanghi, Rapithwina, Uzayeirina, Aiwisruthrima, Aibigaya, and Ushahina are addressed as holy lords of the ritual content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.zoroastrian-avesta-yasna-gathas-mills-archive-l13351-l13415","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/zoroastrian/project-gutenberg/zend-avesta-part-3-yasna-gathas.md","passage_locator":{"label":"YASNA    VII. / YASNA    VII.  223 / YASNA    VII.  2  25 / YASNA    VII.  22  7; lines 13351-13415","start":"13351","end":"13415","translation":"The Zend-Avesta, Part III: The Yasna, Visparad, Afrinagan, Gahs, and Miscellaneous Fragments","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"“And I offer the Haoma and the Haoma-juice for the propitiation of the Fravashi of Zarathustra Spitama the saint… We sacrifice to the Ahuna-vairya, and to the veracious word correctly uttered, and to the good and pious prayer for blessings… (To that one) of beings do we sacrifice whose superior fidelity in the sacrifice Ahura Mazda knows through his Righteousness.”","summary":"The passage is a litany of offerings: the speaker offers Haoma, firewood, perfume, and other elements to the Fravashi of Zarathustra, to Fire as Ahura Mazda’s son, to the Fravashis of saints, to lords of ritual order, and to good heavenly and earthly Yazads. The worshippers pray for a sacred blessing, wish to be known as Ahura Mazda’s praisers and Mathra-speakers, and ask what reward he has appointed to souls, requesting that he bestow this in both this world and the “world of mind” so they may attain his protection and that of Righteousness forever. The commentary also discusses textual structure and numbering of the ‘Seven Chapters’. The liturgical section is headed as praise to Ahura and the Immortals and a prayer for practicing and spreading the faith. The speakers proclaim that they sacrifice to Ahura Mazda, the holy Lord of the ritual order, to the Bountiful Immortals, and to the entire clean creation, both spiritual and mundane, accompanied by the longing blessing of beneficent ritual and of the benignant Mazdayasnian Religion.
