content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.zoroastrian-avesta-yasna-gathas-mills-archive-l19510-l19589","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/zoroastrian/project-gutenberg/zend-avesta-part-3-yasna-gathas.md","passage_locator":{"label":"VISPARAD    IV.  343 / VISPARAD    XI.  351 / VISPARAD    XII.  353 / VISPARAD    XIII.  355; lines 19510-19589","start":"19510","end":"19589","translation":"The Zend-Avesta, Part III: The Yasna, Visparad, Afrinagan, Gahs, and Miscellaneous Fragments","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"\"We strive earnestly, and we take up our Yasna and our homage to the good waters, and to the fertile fruit-trees (which bear as of themselves), and to the Fravashis of the saints...\"","summary":"Liturgical passages of the Visparad describe sacrifices and praise offered to Vohu-khshathra, the \"good kingdom,\" and Khshathra-vairya, the desired kingdom, along with iron-founding and sacrificial words correctly spoken that smite foes and hold the Daevas subject. The text says that reward, health, healing, progress, growth, and victorious smiting are obtained through memorised recital of good thoughts, words, and deeds, which withstand and undo evil and treacherous thoughts, false words, and unfair deeds; it also mentions sacrifice to the later Yasna and the heroic Haptanghaiti. Visparad XXI depicts the worshippers striving earnestly and taking up the Yasna and homage to good waters, fertile fruit-trees that bear as of themselves, the Fravashis of the saints, the Kine, Gaya (Maretan), the Mathra Spenta as a bounteous word-of-reason working within them, and to Ahura Mazda, Zarathustra, Apam-napat, and the Bountiful Immortals. They sacrifice to listening that hears prayers, to mercy that responds to praise, to good praise without hypocrisy or malice, and to the later Yasna itself and its structure. Visparad XXII notes that the fully chanted hymn, together with ceremonial actions, is for the Bountiful Immortals and the holy Saoshyants, described as prophets who shall serve the worshippers.","language":"English","quote_policy":"quoted"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"The worshippers sacrifice to Vohu-khshathra, described as \"the good kingdom,\" and to Khshathra-vairya, \"the kingdom to be desired,\" as well as to iron-founding and to sacrificial words correctly spoken that \"smite (the foe) with victory\" and \"hold the Daevas subject.\"","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"They worship reward, health, healing, progress, growth, and \"victorious smiting\" that are obtained through memorised recital of \"good thoughts, good words, and good deeds\" and used for withstanding evil thoughts, words, and deeds and undoing treacherous thoughts, false words, and unfair deeds.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"They sacrifice to the later Yasna and to the heroic Haptanghaiti, which as it recurs becomes the holy ritual chief.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"In Visparad XXI they \"strive earnestly\" and take up Yasna and homage to the good waters, to fertile fruit-trees \"which bear as of themselves,\" and to the Fravashis of the saints.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"The waters, trees, and Fravashis are explicitly described together as \"those beings which are (so) good.\"","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"They also offer Yasna and homage to the Kine, to Gaya (Maretan), and to the Mathra Spenta, which is called \"the bounteous word-of-reason, the holy, which works (within and for us with effect).\"","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"The same Yasna and homage are directed to Ahura Mazda, to Zarathustra, to the \"lofty lord\" Apam-napat, and to the Bountiful Immortals.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"They sacrifice to \"the listening (that hears our prayers),\" to \"that mercy\" which is shown in response to their offered praise, to a section called fraraiti vidushe in the piece /^adaenais ashaonis, and to \"the good praise which is without hypocrisy, and which has no malice (as its end).\"","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"They sacrifice to the later Yasna, to its offering, and to its chapters, metrical lines, words, and word-structure.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"Visparad XXII states that the fully chanted hymn is \"for the Bountiful Immortals and the holy Saoshyawts (who are the prophets who shall serve us)\" and that it is accompanied by ceremonial actions.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]}],"figures":[{"id":"fig:1","name_or_label":"Ahura Mazda","description":"Deity directly addressed (\"O Ahura Mazda!\") and receiving Yasna and homage along with other honored beings.","role_refs":["role:1"],"evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"fig:2","name_or_label":"Zarathustra","description":"Holy figure addressed (\"O Zarathuitra\") and receiving Yasna and homage alongside Ahura Mazda and other beings.","role_refs":["role:2"],"evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"fig:3","name_or_label":"Bountiful Immortals","description":"Group of immortal beings to whom Yasna and homage are offered and for whom the chant of Visparad XXII is performed.","role_refs":["role:3"],"evidence_refs":["ev:3","ev:5"]},{"id":"fig:4","name_or_label":"Holy Saoshyants","description":"Described explicitly as \"the prophets who shall serve us\" and named as recipients of the chant in Visparad XXII.","role_refs":["role:4"],"evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"fig:5","name_or_label":"Daevas","description":"Hostile beings kept in subjection by correctly spoken sacrificial words that smite foes with victory.","role_refs":["role:5"],"evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"fig:6","name_or_label":"Fravashis of the saints","description":"Spirits of saints named among the good beings to whom Yasna and content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.zoroastrian-avesta-yasna-gathas-mills-archive-l19657-l19784","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/zoroastrian/project-gutenberg/zend-avesta-part-3-yasna-gathas.md","passage_locator":{"label":"VISPARAD    XII.  353 / VISPARAD    XIII.  355 / VISPARAD    XXIII.  363 / AFRINAGAN.; lines 19657-19784","start":"19657","end":"19784","translation":"The Zend-Avesta, Part III: The Yasna, Visparad, Afrinagan, Gahs, and Miscellaneous Fragments","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"The passage explains the Afrinagan blessings as ritual prayers recited over a meal of wine, milk, and fruits prepared in honor of an invited angel or the spirit of a deceased person. A priest performs the consecration, after which the participants eat the meal. These Afrinagan are obligatory for Parsis at fixed times: the six Gahanbar festivals, the five Gatha-days at the end of the year, and the third day (Ardibahist) of the first month (Fravardin), when the Afrinagan Rapithwin is offered to the spirit presiding over the southern quarter, described as guardian of the way to paradise, for any Parsi whose soul wishes to pass the Kinvad bridge after death. The Afrin[-agan] Gahanbar text then begins with a confession of being a Mazda-worshipper of Zarathustra’s order and a foe of the Daevas, and directs sacrifice, homage, propitiation, and praise to various ritual time-lords (Havani, Savanghi, Visya, Asnya, Mahya, Yairya) and to Ritual Righteousness (Asha). The worshippers are told to offer the Myazda of Maidhyo-zaremaya as a piece of sound flesh from a choice beast with a full flow of milk; if this is not possible, they may substitute some suitable liquor, or else bring well-cut, dry wood in appropriate quantities to the Ratu’s house. If even that is impossible, they are to make a mental offering, ascribing sovereign power to Ahura Mazda and to Righteousness, thus completing the sacrifice with a well-timed prayer for blessings. The text commends virtues such as obedience, truthful speech, sanctity, good governance, generosity, and care for the poor. It concludes that if a man fails to give the first or second required Myazda offerings (Maidhyo-zaremaya and Maidhyo-shema), the Ratu who has the right to the offering and guidance over the person expels him from among the Mazda-worshippers as a false disciple comparable to one who does not worship or refuses to recite his vows.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"Afrinagan blessings are recited over a meal consisting of wine, milk, and fruits, prepared in honor of an invited angel or the spirit of a deceased person, and eaten by those present after a priest has performed the consecration.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"The performance of Afrinagan is required of every Parsi at fixed seasons of the year: the six five-day Gahanbars, the five Gatha-days at the end of the year, and the third day (Ardibahist) of the first month (Fravardin).","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"On the third day (Ardibahist) of the first month (Fravardin), the Afrinagan Rapithwin is devoted to the spirit presiding over the southern quarter, described as the guardian of the way to paradise.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"The performance of Afrinagan Rapithwin is enjoined on every Parsi whose soul wants to pass the Kinvad (bridge) after death.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"The speaker in the Afrin Gahanbar text confesses himself a Mazda-worshipper, of Zarathustra’s order, and a foe of the Daevas.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"The text directs sacrifice, homage, propitiation, and praise to Havani and other holy lords of the ritual order such as Savanghi, Visya, Asnya (day-lords), Mahya (month-lords), Yairya (year-lords), the lords of seasons, and to Ritual Righteousness (Asha).","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:3","ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"The Mazdayasnians present the Myazda of Maidhyo-zaremaya by taking a piece of sound flesh from a choice beast with a full flow of milk.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"If the standard flesh-and-milk Myazda cannot be offered, worshippers may take a portion of some liquor of equal value, which is to be properly consumed.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"If the liquid offering is not possible, a man may bring wood of any kind, as long as it is well cut, very dry, and in loads of fitting size, to the Ratu’s house or dwelling and heap it up to specified heights.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"If even bringing wood is not possible, the worshipper is instructed to make a mental offering by ascribing sovereign power to Ahura Mazda, who rules the best, and to Righteousness, thereby completing the sacrifice with a well-timed prayer for blessings.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"The text lists desired qualities of worshippers, including obedience, faithfulness in speech, sanctity, good ordering in the exercise of power, freedom from oppression, rejoicing hearts, generosity, helpfulness to the poor, and fulfillment of ritual.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"The Myazda is described as being offered with a well-timed prayer for These three are described as easy to entreat, desiring to bestow spiritual blessings rather than capricious favor or cruelty, and able to realize their benevolence. The reciter prays that Ahura will fill his desire not with what he personally requests, but with the gifts of Righteousness and divine Benevolence that Ahura knows he needs; these gifts are framed as holy revelation, with the words of the three never void and serving as sustaining power beyond his capacity to ask. Finally, he begs Ahura—set for the defence of Righteous Order and Good Mind—to speak with His \"voice of spirit\" and reveal the laws that pervade and gave rise to the moral universe so that he can declare them to the waiting masses and thereby reform society and relieve the Iranian saint. content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.zoroastrian-avesta-yasna-gathas-mills-archive-l6148-l6191","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/zoroastrian/project-gutenberg/zend-avesta-part-3-yasna-gathas.md","passage_locator":{"label":"YASNA    XXXIII.  75 / YASNA    XXXIII.  77 / YASNA    XXXIII.  79 / YASNA    XXXIV.; lines 6148-6191","start":"6148","end":"6191","translation":"The Zend-Avesta, Part III: The Yasna, Visparad, Afrinagan, Gahs, and Miscellaneous Fragments","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"Translator's commentary on Yasna XXXIV describes how the prophet, in thankfulness for divine gifts such as secured immortality, Righteous Order, and Sovereign Power, resolves to bestow gifts on Ahura. It explains that proper offerings are the actions of a truly pious citizen, along with prayer and songs of praise, rather than sacrificial animals or fruits. A meat-offering is said to be made with homage to Righteous Order and Divine Sovereignty, benefiting sacred settlements, equipping the wise man, and blessing the Immortals and their adherents. The Fire is highlighted as a friendly god of hearth and altar and, more importantly, as priest of the church, invoked for spiritual strength, temporal blessings, and vengeance likened to a thunderbolt. Finally, the commentary expounds the prophet's supplications for God's Kingdom and holy actions, stressing that he seeks to avoid empty ritualism, excessive sacrifices, booty for princes, and gifts for the poet, and instead to nourish God's poor as the essence of Sanctity, Sovereign Authority, and the exalted Kingdom of God.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"The prophet is described as continuing in a tone of thankfulness and declaring that he will bestow gifts upon Ahura according to the measure of the gifts he has received.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"The gifts received from Ahura are stated to be secured Immortality, the Righteous Order, and the Sovereign Power established in holiness and bestowing the Universal Weal.","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"Offerings are said to consist of the actions of a truly pious citizen whose soul is united with Righteousness, along with the homage of prayer and songs of praise, rather than sacrificial beasts or fruits.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"The commentary notes that no piety could exist without strict ecclesiastical regularity, and that ceremonial punctuality is inseparable from honour and charity.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"A meat-offering is described as being offered with homage to the Righteous Order and Divine Sovereignty for the benefit of all sacred settlements, to equip the wise man fully, and as a helpful blessing among the Immortals themselves and their adherents.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"Fire is mentioned as worshipped as the friendly god of the hearth and the altar and, more chiefly, as the priest of the church.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"Fire is called upon for inward spiritual strength, for temporal blessings in various forms, and for vengeance hurled as if in the form of a thunderbolt.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"The prophet is said to supplicate for the coming of the Kingdom and for holy actions, and the commentary clarifies that this does not mean punctilious ritualism apart from charity.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"The prophet rhetorically asks what God's Kingdom is and what kind of prayer he must use so that he may become God's in his actions, explicitly rejecting loading the priesthood with sacrifices, fattening princes with booty, or securing heavy gifts for the poet, and instead aiming to nourish God's poor.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"The commentary states that nourishing God's poor was the essence of the desired Sanctity and Sovereign Authority and of the exalted Kingdom of God.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"The passage observes that Fire is worshipped not so much like Agni as the friendly god of the hearth and altar, but more and chiefly like Agni as the priest of the church.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"The commentary remarks that the prophet does not wish to fatten princes with booty or to secure heavy gifts for the poet, adding a parenthetical note that such abuses occur too often in the 'JZiks'.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]}],"figures":[{"id":"fig:1","name_or_label":"Zarathustra (prophet)","description":"The prophet of the Gathas who, in gratitude for divine gifts, declares that he will bestow gifts on Ahura and rhetorically asks about God's Kingdom and the kind of prayer needed to become God's in his actions.","role_refs":["role:1"],"evidence_refs":["ev:1","ev:5"]},{"id":"fig:2","name_or_label":"Ahura","description":"The deity addressed by the prophet, described as the giver of secured Immortality, Righteous Order, and Sovereign Power, and as the one whose Kingdom, priesthood, princes, poet, and poor are spoken of.","role_refs":["role:2"],"evidence_refs":["ev:1","ev:5"]},{"id":"fig:3","name_or_label":"Righteous Order","description":"A divinely given Order named as one of the gifts received from Ahura and as an entity to which offerings and homage are directed.","role_refs":["role:3","role:4"],"evidence_refs":["ev:1","ev:3"]},{"id":"fig:4","name_or_label":"Sovereign Power / Divine Sovereignty","description":"A divinely given Sovereign Power, established in holiness and bestowing Universal Weal, which is also the object of homage in offerings and associated with Sovereign Authority and the Kingdom of God.","role_refs":["role:3","role:4"],"evidence_refs":["ev:1","ev:3","ev:5"]},{"id":"fig:5","name_or_label":"Immortals","description":"A group of divine beings among whom the meat-offering is described as a helpful blessing, together with their adherents.","role_refs":["role:5"],"evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"fig:6","name_or_label":"Wise man","description":"A wise man who is said to be fully equipped by the meat-offering offered with homage to Righteous Order and Divine The speaker then petitions Mazda, together with Righteous Order and Good Mind, to grant a sign in this life showing how, through sacrifice and devout praise, he may approach the deity. It then praises Him who despised the Daeva-gods and alien men who derided Him, contrasting them with the one who honoured Him, linked with Saoshyant's bounteous Faith and saving power, described as friend, brother, or father to the community. Editorial notes follow, including an introduction to Yasna XLVI that describes it as a sequence of personal sufferings, hopes, and appeals by a leading prophet addressing Ahura and his adherents, and grammatical notes clarifying that the figure who despised the Daevas is likely Ahura.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"Ahura Mazda is described as furthering \"our flocks and men in thrift\" through the good support and bearing of His Good Mind and by His Righteousness.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"The Good Mind is said to provide good support and bearing and is described as \"born in us.\"","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"In the Yasnas of Piety, worshippers seek to praise with homage the one who, through persistent energy, is famed as the Lord Ahura Mazda.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"Ahura Mazda has appointed in His kingdom, through His holy Order and His Good Mind, both Weal and Immortality as an \"eternal mighty pair\" to be granted to the land and the creation.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"The text praises Him who has despised the Daeva-gods and alien men, who had previously held Him in derision.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"The Daeva-gods and alien men are described as far different from the one who gave Ahura honour.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"The one who gave Ahura honour is said to be associated with Saoshyant's bounteous Faith and to be the Lord of saving power, described as a friend, brother, or father to the community, \"Mazda Lord.\"","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:3","ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"The introduction to Yasna XLVI describes the section as dealing with personal sufferings, hopes, and appeals, including verses that are like a \"cry from the depths,\" expressions of animosity, and appeals to warlike adherents and assemblies.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"The same introduction states that the leading prophet is the figure in the first and second verses of Yasna XLVI, that these verses are free from imagery, and that the questions and appeals to Ahura are intended to impress the hearers and animate the reciter.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"A translator's note identifies \"He who despised the Daevas\" as probably Ahura, and explains that the words meaning friend, brother, father are grammatically connected with the one who reverenced Ahura, though the term \"father\" strongly suggests Ahura is referred to.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"A translator's footnote briefly mentions Agni's title \"house-lord\" as a possible comparison but states that this title is not applicable to the Avestan passage under discussion.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]}],"figures":[{"id":"fig:1","name_or_label":"Ahura Mazda (Mazda Lord)","description":"Lord Ahura Mazda, derided Him.","role_refs":["role:1"],"evidence_refs":["ev:1","ev:2","ev:3","ev:5"]},{"id":"fig:2","name_or_label":"Good Mind","description":"The Good Mind, described as providing good support and kingdom.","role_refs":["role:3"],"evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"fig:5","name_or_label":"Weal","description":"Weal, personified as one of the two members of an \"eternal mighty pair\" appointed by Ahura Mazda to be granted to the land and creation.","role_refs":["role:4"],"evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"fig:6","name_or_label":"Immortality","description":"Immortality, personified as one of the This reward is chosen for bodily life through the deeds of the Good Mind working in humans. Those who labor in the toil of the \"mother Kine\" further divine merciful care through understanding and the word of Righteous Order. The speaker then asks Mazda to reveal the best truths, words, actions, and the confessing prayer of the worshipper through the Good Mind and Righteous Order, and petitions that, by sovereign power and IO5 / I06  THE    GATHAS. / YASNA    XLIV.; lines 7520-7561","start":"7520","end":"7561","translation":"The Zend-Avesta, Part III: The Yasna, Visparad, Afrinagan, Gahs, and Miscellaneous Fragments","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"\"Questions asked of Ahura with thankfulness and devotion.\" The piece is said to use the formula, \"This I ask Thee, O Ahura! tell me aright,\" and its verses are described as devotional, moral, polemical, and prophetical.","summary":"Editorial commentary on YASNA XLIV describes it as a composition consisting of questions addressed to Ahura with thankfulness and devotion. The text may have lost some verses or be composed of homogeneous but originally separate fragments, resulting in abrupt transitions that nonetheless do not hinder interpretation. A recurring formula, \"This I ask Thee, O Ahura! tell me aright,\" is noted and is thought to be related to similar wording in Yasna XXXI, 14, possibly indicating later composition, common origin, or derivation between the two pieces. The style of portions of YASNA XLIV is considered homogeneous with hymns confidently ascribed to Zarathustra, and signs of intellectual struggle are taken to point to an early period. The author discusses whether Zarathustra or another member of a narrow circle of religious leaders composed the hymn, considering the level of intellectual cultivation in the wider community, and concludes that Zarathustra most likely composed most of the material, with supplementary fragments written under his dominating influence. The commentator outlines the functions of the verses: 1–2 as an introduction stressing that the ensuing questions are expressions of devotion and occasional appeals for knowledge; 3–5 as questions content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.zoroastrian-avesta-yasna-gathas-mills-archive-l10555-l10599","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/zoroastrian/project-gutenberg/zend-avesta-part-3-yasna-gathas.md","passage_locator":{"label":"YASNA    XLIX.  I  6 / YASNA    XLIX.  165 / YASNA   XLIX.  167 / I  68  THE    GATHAS.; lines 10555-10599","start":"10555","end":"10599","translation":"The Zend-Avesta, Part III: The Yasna, Visparad, Afrinagan, Gahs, and Miscellaneous Fragments","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"A scholarly commentary debates whether Zarathustra personally authored the Gathas or whether an unnamed superior \"prime mover\" did. It cites formulae like \"to Zarathmtra and to us\" and the phrase glossed as \"may he declare my regulations\" to argue about authorship and authority. The commentator considers a hypothetical unnamed individual, mentally and personally superior to Zarathustra and his associates Vutaspa, Frashaortra, and Gamaspa, as the real author and \"power behind both throne and home,\" then questions this hypothesis by asking whether a founder of a religion or a popular religious composer would designate another as \"chosen of God\" and as the life of the community's faith if that person were not truly central. The passage concludes that Zarathustra, who has the leading name and composed hymns, likely held real prominence over the other named figures.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"The passage cites the expression \"to Zarathmtra and to us\" from Yasna XXVIII, 7.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"Zarathmtra is said to be named as \"mahya razeng sahi/,\" glossed as \"may he declare my regulations.\"","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"The commentator states that the request \"may he declare my regulations\" could literally be spoken only by a superior, possibly by the \"prime mover\" himself.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"The text raises the question whether the verses in question were written by the \"prime mover\" and whether this prime mover was different from Zarathmtra.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"One hypothesis proposes that, if the prime mover wrote these verses, then either he wrote the entire mass of the Gathas or the Gathas were composed by four or five closely connected individuals.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"Although some verses are acknowledged as products of secondary persons, the Gathas are described as essentially \"one man's work, directly or indirectly.\"","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"The present section is characterised as \"especially original in its tone.\"","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"If the present section were not by Zarathmtra, the person whose \"heart and soul\" and \"power\" were in Zarathmtrianism would be, according to the commentator, an unnamed individual more important than Zarathmtra.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"Under that hypothesis, the prominence of Zarathmtra's name is attributed to his personal activity supported by the social rank of the Spitamas.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"In the same hypothetical scenario, Zarathmtra is described as \"a princely disciple, ... and nothing more.\"","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"The commentator argues that, in this hypothesis, the \"real author of Zarathmtrianism\" would be \"in no sense Zarathmtra,\" nor Vutaspa, nor Frashaortra, nor Gamaspa, noting that Gamaspa is addressed in the vocative.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"The hypothetical unnamed individual is described as mentally and personally superior to Zarathmtra, Vutaspa, Frashaortra, and Gamaspa.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:13","text":"This unnamed superior is characterised as \"the power behind both throne and home,\" yet remaining without a name.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:14","text":"The text questions whether the founder of a religion, or of a new departure in a religion, would describe another person as \"the chosen of God\" if that person were not supposed to be highly eminent.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:15","text":"The commentary asks whether a popular and sincerely enthusiastic religious composer, about to chant a hymn before a meeting of religious masses, would name a person whom the crowds did not regard as \"the life of their religious     "summary": "Mills introduces Yasna XXVIII as prayers primarily seeking grace and revelation. He explains that Zarathustra, having entered his office, composes a liturgy for eminent colleagues and a reciter-priest, who stands with hands extended toward Ahura or His Fire, praying for spiritual gifts to ease the grief of the Kine's Soul. The reciter approaches Ahura Mazda, inspired by the Good Mind, asking for bodily and spiritual boons derived from personified Righteousness, which can establish the elect in a beatified state. The personalities of the Amesha Spentas—Righteousness (Asha), Good Mind (Vohu Manah), Khshathra as divine sovereignty, and Aramaiti as practical piety—are invoked to come, like Vedic gods, to aid the supplicant and his worship, which is seen as the effective means of redemption. The reciter offers his soul to heaven, seeks experiential knowledge of the blessed rewards granted through ceremonial and moral actions prescribed by Ahura Mazda, vows to continue teaching to spread the Religious Order, and fervently asks personified Righteousness for vision and fuller knowledge of the Good Mind, the way to God, and Obedience, treating these abstractions as persons.",

content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.zoroastrian-avesta-yasna-gathas-mills-archive-l10129-l10200","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/zoroastrian/project-gutenberg/zend-avesta-part-3-yasna-gathas.md","passage_locator":{"label":"I56  THE    GATHAS. / YASNA    XLVIII.  157 / YASNA    XLIX.  159 / YASNA  XLIX.; lines 10129-10200","start":"10129","end":"10200","translation":"The Zend-Avesta, Part III: The Yasna, Visparad, Afrinagan, Gahs, and Miscellaneous Fragments","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"\"A border chief, B^wdva by name, had proved himself too formidable ... and the holy Faith knows how to beg for vengeance on the armed Dru^-worshipper.\"","summary":"Mills' commentary on Yasna XLIX describes reverses and hopes in a holy cause aligned with Asha, including a struggle that went against the righteous party. Footnotes explain Aramaiti's association with pastures, husbandmen, and the earth, and a Pahlavi interpretation that speaks of enforced quiet and a finishing blow to the wicked. The main discussion portrays a border chief B^wdva as a formidable armed Dru^-worshipper who leads a settled rival religious system with functionaries and judicial authority, opposing the true prophet and Zarathustrian Piety. Invective condemns a priestly judge serving Drug-worshippers as a cheat and foe to the holy Order, repudiating holy counsel as the source of pious wisdom. The commentary further emphasizes cosmic dualism between Righteous Order and the Lie-demon, with no compromise possible, and describes the poet's appeal to divine Benevolence or a chief representing the Good Mind as guardian, while placing an interdict on the throng adhering to the Lie-demon and linking them closely with Daeva-worshippers.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"The heading to Yasna XLIX characterizes the chapter as \"Reverses and Hopes\" and mentions honour to Frashaostra and other chiefs.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"The

content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.zoroastrian-avesta-yasna-gathas-mills-archive-l6809-l6904","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/zoroastrian/project-gutenberg/zend-avesta-part-3-yasna-gathas.md","passage_locator":{"label":"YASNA   XLIII.  91 / THE    GATHA(A)    U-STAVAITI(I). / YASNA    XLIII.  93 / YASNA   XLIII.; lines 6809-6904","start":"6809","end":"6904","translation":"The Zend-Avesta, Part III: The Yasna, Visparad, Afrinagan, Gahs, and Miscellaneous Fragments","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"Scholarly commentary on Yasna XLIII describes it as announcing salvation as universal for believers and as containing Zarathustra’s reflections on the sublimity and bountifulness of Ahura. The commentator analyzes the structure of the verses (1–3 as preliminary, 4–6 on Ahura’s power and benevolence with allusions to final judgment, 7–15 on the prophet’s call prompted by Sraosha, and 16 as a possibly later closing strophe). A Pahlavi translator’s suggestion is cited: the opening line might mean “Salvation to him to whom there is salvation for every man,” which, along with other possibilities, frames a prayer where the composer beseeches Ahura for “two mighty and eternal ones”: universal wholeness or welfare of soul and body, and the unlimited duration of that blessed condition. These two blessings, sought along with splendour, are said to be requested not selfishly but to maintain Asha, the religious Order underpinning sacred polity, wealth, and individual sanctity. The text further calls this the highest good and adds a prayer for “maya,” compared to the supernatural wisdom of an “Indian Hercules” but here interpreted as the mysterious wisdom of Divine Benevolence. Another highest blessing is described as the attainment of “the one who guides to the straight paths,” identified with the way—namely, the conceptions and revelations of the Saviours—where the believer prospers and where Ahura dwells as in his kingdom and chosen home. The commentary wonders whether “this man who shows the paths” of the bodily and mental world is the same figure as the one who prays for boons of the two worlds in another Yasna passage, perhaps Zarathustra himself, and raises the question whether Zarathustra was the only sacred singer or the central figure of a group.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"The heading presents Yasna XLIII as announcing salvation as universal for believers and as containing reflections of Zarathustra on the sublimity and bountifulness of Ahura.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"The commentary states that verses 1–3 are preliminary, verses 4–6 describe power and benevolence in the Deity with allusions to the final judgment, verses 7–15 reflect on the prophet’s call uttered at the instigation of Sraosha, and verse 16 is a closing strophe that may be a later addition.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"A Pahlavi translator suggests the line may mean “Salvation to him to whom there is salvation for every man,” which the commentator treats as a possible reading that would avoid assuming lost verses.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"The commentator entertains the alternative that some laudatory verses may have been lost, comparing the possible missing content to Yasna XXXIV, 14, which speaks of a “princely priest” devoted to Ahura and receiving salvation.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"The composer is described as beseeching Ahura to grant “two mighty and eternal ones” that complement each other: universal wholeness and welfare of soul and body, and the unlimited duration of that blessed condition.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"These “two mighty and eternal ones” are also called the “powerful and continuous two” and are associated with a term whose equivalent later designated the Bountiful Immortals.","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"The “powerful and continuous two” are sought together with splendour as rewards not for selfish gratification but to maintain Asha, the religious Order, on which sacred polity, tribal and national wealth, and especially the individual sanctity of life depend.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"The commentary identifies this combination of blessings and their purpose as the highest good.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"A prayer is added for “maya,” which is said to recall the supernatural wisdom of the “Indian Hercules,” but in this text is interpreted as the mysterious wisdom of Divine Benevolence, described as colourless and abstract yet religiously deep.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"The highest blessing is again described as “the better than the good,” defined as the attainment of “the one who guides to the straight paths.”","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"The “straight paths” are explained as the way consisting of the conceptions and revelations of the Saviours, in which the believer prospers and in which Ahura dwells as in his kingdom and “chosen home.”","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"The commentary asks whether “this man who shows the paths” of the bodily and mental world is the same as the one who prays for boons of the two worlds in Yasna XXVIII, 3, and whether he is Zarathustra, suggesting that Zarathustra may have composed both passages and sometimes refers to himself in the third person.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:13","text":"The commentator questions whether Zarathustra was the sole sacred singer or the central figure of a group of sacred singers, mentioning the name Gamaspa Hvogva from Yasna XLVI, 17.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:9"]},{"id":"obs:14","text":"The commentary explicitly characterizes the religious conceptions in the passage as rich and deep.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]}],"figures":[{"id":"fig:1","name_or_label":"Ahura","description":"The benevolent Deity whose sublimity and bountifulness are praised, who grants {"record_id":"batch.motif.zoroastrian-avesta-yasna-gathas-mills-archive-l4879-l4981","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/zoroastrian/project-gutenberg/zend-avesta-part-3-yasna-gathas.md","passage_locator":{"label":"YASNA    XXXI.  51 / YASNA    XXXI. / YASNA  XXXII. / YASNA   XXXII.  55; lines 4879-4981","start":"4879","end":"4981","translation":"The Zend-Avesta, Part III: The Yasna, Visparad, Afrinagan, Gahs, and Miscellaneous Fragments","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"Commentary on Yasna XXXII.55 describes the composer denouncing wretched delinquents and an apostate (Yima), warning of imminent destruction known only to Ahura. An unnamed opposing leader undermines the composer’s teachings, blasphemes the Sun and the mystical Kine (holy herds and people), harms productive land, and murders saints. The composer laments slaughter, spiritual opposition, plots by powerful persons, and illegal confiscation of inheritances, and he asserts that his opponents injure his adherents. He proclaims God’s solemn judgment, highlighting treachery against the mystical Kine and choices between GrAma and Asha, and between the kingdom of the Lie-demon and the Divine Khshathra. Gndima, an opposing chief, desires the evil kingdom in personified Hell and envies the holy apostleship, but the messenger of God will keep him from Divine Righteousness and exclude him from the Faith.

Editorial remarks describe a bitter doctrinal struggle, including battle imagery of two hosts closing for holy vows, repeated "judicial blindness," and a conflict between a Daeva-party and the Zarathustrians, two parties outwardly similar in faith yet divided over dualism. Pagans are said to implicate gods in their sins, with a comparison to "the drunken Indra," and a war of doctrines is fought with both speech and weapons.

Further commentary deplores the Kavis, who aid the opposing party with stratagems and false teachings and claim the Kine will be injured, not blessed, by the fire-priest who kindles the altar-flame. The composer, however, is sustained by hope that he and his fellow-labourers will be borne to heaven by personified Weal and Immortality, the "eternal two" who bear saints to bliss and constitute heaven’s beatitude. Ultimately he entrusts all to Ahura, who controls events, resolves doubts, and supports his servants in bringing the wicked to vengeance through verbal instructions. A reconstructed translation mentions a rival monarch for whom plots are laid to secure sovereignty; once in power he would deliver home, village, town, and province to ruin and death.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"The composer contemplates with religious irony the wretched delinquents he addresses, stating that none of them knows the destruction that awaits them and is close at hand, while Ahura knows of it and it will be proportionately severe; he views their blindness to danger and to truth as a form of judgment.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"The composer names the apostate Yima, whom he believes first introduced the consumption of the flesh of cattle, and he disavows any community with Yima or the delinquents, declaring himself separate from them in Ahura’s sight.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"The composer states that the opponents’ leader has to some degree defeated his teachings and impaired the just estimates of life he tried to instill in the people, has made inroads on his property dedicated to the holy cause, and that he cries aloud to Ahura and Asha with the words of his soul.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"The composer repeats that the opponents’ leader threatens to invalidate his teachings, blasphemes the Sun as the supreme object of nature and the sacred Kine, injures the productive land, and carries murder among the saints.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"The composer utters a bitter wail over attempted slaughter and spiritual opposition, points out plots among the powerful and their illegal confiscation of inheritances belonging to women and men, and declares that his opponents seek to injure his adherents, reacting against their best spiritual qualities.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"The composer announces the solemn judgment of God on these actions, condemns those who deal treacherously with the mystical Kine, defined as the holy herds and people, and addresses those who prefer the GrAma over saving and sanctifying Asha and the Kingdom of the Lie-demon over the Divine Khshathra.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"The composer says that Gndima, an opposing chief, desires the evil kingdom in the abode of the personified Hell and enviously wishes to share in the holy apostleship, but that the messenger of God will keep him far from the sight of Divine Righteousness, so he can have no share in the Faith.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"Editorial commentary notes that the text provides data on the struggle, mentioning in another passage a battle where two hosts close in regular lines for the holy vows, and here emphasizing willing complaint or regretful desire and repeated references to judicial blindness.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"The editor suggests that the Daeva-party closely resembles the Zarathustrians in many religious peculiarities but cannot accept or understand the dualism; he remarks that Pagans implicate the gods in their sins and adds the parenthetical comparison to the drunken Indra, describing a bitter and violent war of doctrines fought with both speech and weapons between two parties, each claiming to represent a similar outward form of faith.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"The composer deplores the establishment of the Kavis, who use stratagems and false teachings to aid the opposing party, and reports that they say the Kine herself will be injured instead of blessed by the fire-priest who kindles the altar-flame.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:9"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"The composer supports himself with hope of ultimate success and reward, anticipating that he and his fellow-labourers will be gloriously borne to heaven by Weal and Immortality, described as the eternal two who bear saints to bliss and constitute the beatitude of heaven.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:10"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"The composer entrusts everything to Ahura, described as able to control all events and solve all doubts, who will support his servants in bringing the wicked to vengeance through verbal instructions and commands.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:11"]},{"id":"obs:13","text":"The reconstructed translation mentions a rival monarch, for whom some plot to secure sovereignty, who if he attained power would deliver home, village, town, and province to ruin and death, and who is active in his efforts.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:12"]},{"id":"obs:14","text":"The mystical Kine is explicitly explained as representing holy herds and people.","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:15","text":"Hell is described as personified and as the abode of the evil kingdom desired by Gndima.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:16","text":"Weal and Immortality are described as the eternal two who both carry saints to heavenly bliss and themselves constitute the beatitude of heaven.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:10"]},{"id":"obs:17","text":"The editor notes that dualism is a key doctrinal issue that the Daeva-party cannot accede to or understand.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:18","text":"The struggle is characterized as involving two hosts and two parties closing in battle lines and waging a violent war of doctrines.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]}],"figures":[{"id":"fig:1","name_or_label":"Composer of the Gathas","description":"Unnamed composer who addresses delinquents and
